notion.title: Cabaret l'Enfer Review: Tasting Menu, Chef's Counter, and What to Know

metadata.Meta title: Cabaret l'Enfer, the Plateau: An Honest Review
metadata.Meta desc: Massimo Piedimonte's Michelin-listed tasting menu on Saint-Denis. Careful cooking, a loud room, small portions, and why it wasn't my favourite night out.
metadata.Price range: $$$$. Tasting menu about $165. I paid $250 with one cocktail, tax and tip.
metadata.Hours: Tue to Sat from 6pm, closed Sun and Mon. 33 seats, OpenTable only.

blocks.text: REVIEW · THE PLATEAU
Chef Massimo Piedimonte cooks a modern Quebecois tasting menu on Saint-Denis, in a black-walled 33-seat room in the Plateau that plays rock loud enough to drown out the dish descriptions.
By Victor · Published [DATE] · Checked September 2026
NOT OUR FIRST PICK
Careful cooking, hard room, and a bill that asks a lot

Nothing here is badly made. The ferments are interesting, the ingredients are good, and the hour at the counter was the best part of the night. What I didn't get was the one course you're still thinking about the next morning, and at $165 before drinks that's the thing I'm paying for. For the same money in Montreal I'd book somewhere else. If you go, take the counter, go with someone you can already hear, and don't come hungry expecting to leave full.

rows: The view over the pass lets you watch the team plate each course. The counter is more compelling than the food itself.
Service starts at 6pm and the table runs three hours, so this is the whole evening rather than the end of one.
Loud enough that four people works better than two, but the three-hour limit means you're committed.
You'll spend the evening leaning across the table, and you're locked into a fixed seven-course run before you know if you like each other.
For a milestone I'd want a quieter room where conversation is easier.
$165 before you've had a drink. Nothing about this is casual.

blocks.text: Black walls, waxed concrete, white-painted brick with two dark canvases on it, a long banquette, warm wood tables and tan leather chairs. Candlelight pools on a black counter that bounces all of it back at you. The menu arrives inside an envelope closed with a wax seal, which is a fun way to start a night.

The music is the thing to know before you book. Rock and skate punk, turned up, and clearly turned up on purpose. It's loud enough that I couldn't hear the dish descriptions, which at this price is a real part of the experience going missing. If that sounds like a good dinner you'll have a good time. If you were picturing candlelight and easy conversation, pick somewhere else.
No dress code worth worrying about. Smart casual covers it.
[PORTRAIT: Massimo Piedimonte. 200 x 240. Photo credit needed.]
Massimo Piedimonte came up through Le Mousso, Maison Boulud and Noma before opening his own room. He competed on Top Chef: Destination Canada in 2025 and finished fifth.
[PULL QUOTE NEEDED. One line in the chef's own words, on why this dish or why this neighbourhood. Recorded speech only, so this stays empty until there's an interview.]

The name is an homage rather than a description. It borrows from the Cabaret de l'Enfer, the hell-themed room in Montmartre that ran from 1892 until around 1950, and the seven courses are loosely framed around the seven deadly sins. What you can actually taste is the fermentation program. There's a shelf of jars in view from the counter, labelled and dated by hand, one of them a rose starter from July marked to be racked on 22 September. That shelf is the clearest statement of intent in the room, and it's the part of the cooking I'd come back for.
[LINK: Massimo Piedimonte's recipe card, for your kitchen. Needs the interview first.]
Order the first drink before you open the menu.

To start — I had a negroni. It wasn't presented or suggested; I had to ask for it. Bitter, low sugar, and good. I couldn't tell whether it was a regular option or part of a rotating cocktail selection because nobody explained the list.

With the meal — the pairing, at about $120. The person I was with took it, so I saw how it went. Bottles presented, wine poured, not much said about any of it. No producer, no region, no reason why a given glass sat beside a given course. At that price the explanation is a good chunk of what you're buying.
Not drinking — no alternatives were presented. Nobody mentioned mocktails or other non-alcoholic options, so I can't tell you what was available.
I wasn't given a proper presentation of the cocktails, so I can't tell you how broad the list is or whether it rotates.

The dining room serves one seasonal tasting menu: seven courses plus bread and snacks for the whole table, around $165 a head at last check. The terrace runs à la carte in summer; the dining room doesn't.

THE WAITER'S CHOICE — omitted. Nobody made a recommendation worth repeating, and with a fixed menu there's nothing to recommend. The template says leave this block out rather than invent one, so it's out.
I could not hear the dish descriptions. I caught three names and lost the rest. What follows is what I can name and what I can see in my photos.
Cappellacci, nordic shrimp, lacto koji
Folded green pasta parcels in a shallow bowl, raw nordic shrimp laid over the top, a pale foam over that. The lacto koji is the fun part and this kitchen is good at that sort of thing.
Ora King salmon, "divorciado"

A block of salmon split down the middle by two sauces, bright green on one side, deep red-orange on the other, one small shellfish alongside. The name winks at huevos divorciados, two sauces that never meet. Best-looking plate of the night.
"Amy Winehouse," rhubarb, citron basilic

A white disc in a wide bowl with a portrait stencilled onto it in dark powder. The rhubarb and citron basilic were part of the same dessert. They do these music tributes, and there's a Leonard Cohen one too.
[FOUR MORE COURSES, NAMES UNCONFIRMED]

From my photos: slices of otoro. A canapé of otoro with microgreens on a dark base. Three crisp rolled tubes filled with something red on a pewter bowl. A dessert I couldn't identify in a white bowl. A dish of barigoule vegetables finished with a cougar stencil. Describe or name them properly once you have a menu card.

One pattern worth flagging. A golden disc alone in a bowl. A white disc with a stencil. Barigoule vegetables under a cougar stencil. Round, flat, centred, decorated on top. Three of the seven came out as a version of the same idea. Any one of them looks great; three in a row and I started to clock it. Plenty of people won't notice, but it took a bit of the surprise out of the sequence.
I paid $250 all in for the set menu, one cocktail, tax and tip. The person I was with took the wine pairing, which wasn't part of my total.

rows: About $120 extra; the person I was with took it

blocks.text: The portions were noticeably smaller than at other tasting menus I've tried, and all of us left hungry. A good tasting menu should send you out comfortably full. This one didn't. Line up somewhere to eat after.
Victor · one visit, September 2026 · paid for it
The part that's just my opinion
The hour at the counter was the best part of the night. Watching four people build plates a tweezer-load at a time held my attention. I'd sit there again. I'm less sure I'd pay $165 for the menu.

The honest caveat is the service. Our server was new and it showed: he couldn't tell us much about the cocktail or where the wine came from, and on the pairing the bottles arrived, got poured, and that was that. Everyone starts somewhere and that sorts itself out in a few months, so I'd believe anyone who tells me their night was sharper. But on the night I paid, it was the difference between a good meal and a good evening.

blocks.text: SLOT EMPTY. Every review closes on the same question to the chef: what would you make for a date night at home? The answer becomes the recipe card, and it's the same question that closes their chef page, so the two pages meet. This needs an interview with Piedimonte. Until then the slot stays visibly empty rather than filled with something plausible.
How far ahead do I need to book?
Not far. A table for two was easy to get. It's OpenTable only, 33 seats, with a three-hour table limit, so a bigger group is a different problem.
Can they handle dietary restrictions?

lines: Verdict state is a judgement call. John set this to pass, Not our first pick, on 23 Sept 2026. The case for a softer conditional was: your criticisms were the room, the price and one new server, and you wrote yourself that a sharper night would track. The case for pass, Not our first pick: you said not your favourite and you're not rushing to rebook. The verdict line, the essentials card and the Impressing a cook row were rewritten to match.
Michelin. The plaque in your photo says MICHELIN 2026, which is a Guide listing, not a star. No star. Never imply one.
Top Chef. Fifth place on Destination Canada, not the winner. Named in Meet the chef as a placing, which is accurate.
$165 is from a March 2026 report; the restaurant publishes no price. Your $250 is solid because you paid it. Hedged as "at last check".

Five things this template needs that we don't have: the chef pull quote, the recipe card answer, the Google rating snapshot, two Make a night of it spots, and two of the three FAQ answers. The first two need an interview. The rest are a phone call and an afternoon.
Word count is roughly 1,250, over the 1,000 floor but short of the 1,865 this layout expects. The gap is Meet the chef, which runs on research rather than an interview.
